Why cactusFeedSandy ValleyBioenergyWater valueNewsPartners

Rural America needs ways to keep farming where water is running short.

Desert Cactus Fuels works with farmers to grow spineless cactus in dry regions. The crop supplies livestock feed, creates a local source of biomass for renewable fuels, and reduces water use when it replaces thirsty crops. Together, those uses create new income while keeping land in production and is protecting aquifers and the Colorado River.

Feed, fuel and water savings

Feed

Chopped cactus pads can supply moisture and digestible energy as part of a balanced ration for cattle, sheep or goats.

Fuel

Cactus biomass can go to an anaerobic digester to produce biogas, which can be used locally or upgraded to renewable gas.

Water savings

In a FAO-published arid-zone comparison, Opuntia produced a kilogram of crop dry matter with about 73% less water than alfalfa.

The idea

One crop, more than one use.

Desert Cactus Fuels is building a local supply chain around spineless prickly pear: grow it, use it in livestock feed right away, and grow it as biomass for bioenergy.

The crop's dryland physiology makes the model especially interesting where irrigation is expensive or scarce. The strongest projects use suitable dryland acreage, nearby feed demand and a local outlet for bioenergy biomass.

The water advantage

A different equation from alfalfa.

In a FAO-published arid-zone comparison, Opuntia produced a kilogram of crop dry matter with about 73% less water than alfalfa. That points to a valuable option for farms facing tighter irrigation supplies.

Published crop comparison, not a guarantee for every field. Cactus also has a different nutrient profile, so feed rations must be balanced.

Livestock feed

Useful forage when water is limited.

Chopped cactus pads can supply moisture and digestible energy as part of a balanced ration for cattle, sheep or goats. This is a practical feed ingredient for dry regions, backed by decades of use and research.

What it brings to the ration

Moisture

Fresh pads carry water into the feed, valuable during dry periods.

Energy

Digestible carbohydrates add a useful component to forage mixes.

Flexibility

Studies have replaced part of an alfalfa-based ration with cactus while retaining other nutrients in the diet.

Cactus is an ingredient, not a complete replacement for alfalfa's protein and fibre. See the FAO feeding studies ↗

Demonstrated in Chile

Up to 30%of alfalfa hay replaced in a published goat ration study

That result shows how cactus can earn a place in a formulated diet. The right blend depends on the animals and the tested feed.

Read the study ↗
Dryland field · image from Desert Cactus Fuels

Made for local production

Grow close to the animals that need it.

Cactus is a wet crop, so distance matters. A project works best when land, feed processing and livestock demand are connected locally.

Start with a pilot field and a real feed buyer. Measure yield, water use and feed quality, then scale the model that works.

Growing biomass for bioenergy

Feed today. Biomass for bioenergy too.

Feed is the immediate use: cactus pads go into balanced livestock rations. Beyond feed, spineless cactus can be grown as a biomass crop for bioenergy on dryland acreage.

Cactus biomass can go to an anaerobic digester, potentially with livestock manure, to produce biogas. The remaining digestate may have agricultural use. Published research has demonstrated this route with Opuntia waste. With a nearby operator, biogas can be used locally or upgraded to renewable gas.

A third opportunity

Less water in. More value out.

Where replacing irrigated forage with cactus creates a real, measurable saving in the local basin, that water benefit may help a partner offset its usage or meet a replenishment target.

Make the saving count.

The project needs a credible baseline, measured water use and a benefit that stays in the catchment. An eligible volume can then be assessed and independently verified under the applicable program.

The opportunity is real, but a particular farm's offset value is established by its own measurements and program rules.

Colorado River · Agriculture

Alfalfa alone uses more Colorado River water than all cities and industry combined.

Agriculture consumes about 10 million acre-feet of Colorado River water each year. Alfalfa alone consumes about 5 million acre-feet, more than the roughly 3.5 million acre-feet consumed by all municipal, commercial and industrial users combined. They show where large, lasting savings are possible.
